column3: The Hebrew uses collective singular horse and chariotry; BSB uses plural “their horses and chariots.”
The Hebrew includes the speech formula “Thus said Ben-hadad” here; BSB places it in the next verse.
The Hebrew starts with the demand for silver and gold; BSB places the speech introduction before it in this verse. The Hebrew says “sons,” where BSB uses “children.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew gives the demand as “you shall give me”; BSB makes it the purpose of sending and uses “children” for “sons.”
The Hebrew says “your house,” “the desire of your eyes,” and “their hand”; BSB uses “your palace,” “all that is precious to you,” and “seize.”
The Hebrew says “my sons”; BSB uses “my children.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the respondent unnamed and the final recipient pronominal; BSB supplies Ahab and Ben-hadad.
The Hebrew leaves the recipient unnamed and describes the people as “at my feet”; BSB supplies Ahab and uses “my men.”
The Hebrew says “the one girding” and “the one loosening,” without naming armor; BSB supplies “armor.”
The Hebrew leaves Ben-hadad unnamed and says that he heard the word; BSB names him and says he received the message.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew names Ahab only in the opening question; BSB names him again later and supplies “the prophet” for both replies.
The Hebrew leaves the mustering subject unnamed and calls the second group “all the people, all the sons of Israel”; BSB supplies Ahab and uses “the rest of the Israelite troops.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew does not name what Ben-hadad sent out; BSB supplies “scouts.”
Close to the Hebrew.

Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “strengthen yourself” and “at the return of the year”; BSB uses “strengthen your position” and “in the spring.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew names governors as replacements for the kings; BSB uses “other officers.”
The Hebrew leaves the opponents and the listening king unnamed and says that he listened to their voice; BSB supplies the Israelites and the king and says he approved their plan.
The Hebrew says “at the return of the year” and uses collective “Aram”; BSB says “in the spring” and “the Arameans.”
The Hebrew uses passive forms for being mustered and provided for; BSB describes mobilizing and gathering supplies actively.
The Hebrew repeats the saying formula and says that Aram “said”; BSB combines the formula and uses “think.”
The Hebrew says “these opposite these,” without explicitly naming armies; BSB supplies “the armies.”
The Hebrew says he came to a room within a room; BSB adds the action “hid” and condenses the rooms as “an inner room.”
